question: HANDOFF-T2.md §4 item A left one sub-question open: the body of Adaptive-Forgetting.md line 171 says 'Anderson (1996), Journal of Experimental Psychology: General [1]' while reference [1] is Nature. The handoff proposed the fix might be to 'correct to the real 1991 JEP:General paper' -- Anderson & Green (1991), 'Self-monitoring and suppression of memories', JEP:General 120(3), 3-31 -- and said to verify it independently before choosing between re-dating to 2001 Nature and correcting to a 1991 JEP:General paper. THIS NOTE RESOLVES IT.
verdict: The handoff's proposed 1991 substitute is ITSELF fabricated. Both options in the handoff are wrong. The correct action is the re-attribution the handoff described as option 1, plus one correction the handoff did not anticipate: the line-171 journal attribution is a SECOND, independent error that must also be fixed, because re-dating alone would leave 'Journal of Experimental Psychology: General' attached to a Nature paper.

finding_1_the_1991_paper_does_not_exist.conclusion: 'Self-monitoring and suppression of memories' by Anderson & Green is not a real paper. No source prints it.
finding_1_the_1991_paper_does_not_exist.evidence_a_page_collision: JEP:General vol 120 issue 3 is continuously occupied across pages 235-328 by real, individually identified articles. The handoff's own claimed span 3-31 is impossible twice over: (i) issue 3 does not begin at page 3 -- issue 1 occupies pp. 3-119 -- so '120(3), 3-31' is internally incoherent on its face; (ii) the alternative reading '261-273' is not free either. Graesser, Lang & Roberts (1991) 'Question answering in the context of stories' occupies JEP:General 120:254-277, which CONTAINS 261-273. Two papers cannot share pages in one issue. The 254-277 span was independently corroborated outside Crossref, from a third-party bibliography in the LREC 2020 computational-models-of-narrative volume, which prints 'Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 120:254-277'.
finding_1_the_1991_paper_does_not_exist.evidence_b_title_absent_everywhere: An exact-phrase search for 'self-monitoring and suppression of memories' returns no matching title in any index. Every hit is a different, real suppression paper (Anderson & Green 2001 Nature; Bergstrom; Depue; Bulevich). The phrase appears in no reference list surfaced by search.
finding_1_the_1991_paper_does_not_exist.evidence_c_no_anderson_in_1991: Neither Crossref nor PubMed returns ANY Anderson item in JEP:General for 1991. PubMed holds 15 such records for the year and Crossref 37 unique DOIs; both indexes are independently incomplete (PubMed is missing the Graesser article, and Crossref issue 4 holds only 3 articles), so this absence is corroborating rather than decisive -- which is exactly why the page collision in (a) carries the argument.

method_and_its_traps.principle: A 404 from a resolver is evidence about the resolver, not about the paper, unless the resolver's coverage for that journal/year has been measured first.
method_and_its_traps.coverage_measured_before_trusting_any_ne: Crossref 1991 JEP:General = 37 unique DOIs across 4 issues, with issue 4 containing only 3 articles. A flagship psychology journal publishes far more than that per year, so the deposit is demonstrably partial. PubMed J Exp Psychol Gen 1991 = 15 records, and it omits the Graesser article that certainly exists. Conclusion: neither index can refute a paper by absence.
traps_hit_and_avoided: TRAP 7.7 (a zero from a search API is evidence about the query until a control says otherwise). I ran a positive control on EVERY endpoint before reading any zero. Crossref control (10.1038/35066572) returned the real Anderson & Green 2001 Nature paper, so Crossref was live and its 404s carried weight. PubMed control (Anderson MC[au] AND J Exp Psychol Gen[ta]) returned only 4 records, earliest 2001 -- which is what first revealed that PubMed's pre-2001 coverage is thin, rather than proving absence.

The first delegated researcher returned a confident 'PHANTOM, does not exist' verdict based on Crossref 404 + Semantic Scholar not-found. That verdict was NOT accepted: it rested on exactly the incomplete-coverage evidence above, and it was reached without the coverage measurement that would have discredited it. It happened to reach the right conclusion for partly wrong reasons, which is the dangerous kind of right.

OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar both returned HTTP 429 to this host on every attempt with escalating backoff (10s, 20s, 30s, 40s, 50s, 60s). Their empty result sets were TOOLING FAILURE and were explicitly not read as literature findings. A second researcher was dispatched to non-API routes (Google Scholar, third-party bibliographies) for that reason.

doi.org content negotiation was also rejected as an instrument: it returned 404 for the KNOWN-GOOD 10.1038/35066572 and 403 for a real Crossref DOI in the same batch, i.e. it was measuring bot-blocking, not existence.

APA PsycNet is Incapsula-blocked from this host ('Request unsuccessful. Incapsula incident ID') and never returned a table of contents; the browser route failed too (Chrome profile lock). The page-collision argument was therefore built from Crossref's issue-level pagination plus an external corroborating bibliography, not from the publisher's own TOC.

corrected_diagnosis_of_the_two_errors.error_1_the_phantom_paper: There is no Anderson (1996), Nature 379(6565):232-236. Confirmed absent via PubMed (which indexes Nature independently of Crossref) with a positive control before and after. The real paper is Anderson & Green (2001), Nature 410(6826):366-369, DOI 10.1038/35066572, which the file ALREADY cites correctly at line 22 and reference [2].
corrected_diagnosis_of_the_two_errors.error_2_the_journal_misattribution: Line 171 says 'Journal of Experimental Psychology: General' and calls the work 'The original RIF demonstration'. Reference [1] is Nature. The handoff anticipated this ('the file may have a second journal error, not just a bad year') and it is confirmed. Note the claim is additionally mischaracterised: the 2001 Nature paper is an fMRI think/no-think suppression study, NOT the original behavioural RIF demonstration -- the file itself describes it that way at line 178-185. So the file's reference [1] entry, which describes the 1996 paper as 'the founding study of Retrieval-Induced Forgetting' and reports behavioural design details (category-member pairs, Rp+/Rp-/Ur, ~40% recall reduction, d~0.65/0.47), is describing behavioural work that the 2001 fMRI paper does not contain.
corrected_diagnosis_of_the_two_errors.consequence_for_the_fix: Blindly re-dating 1996 -> 2001 would make the file assert that a 2001 fMRI paper reported behavioural RIF effect sizes. That is a wrong citation with correct metadata, which §4 of the handoff explicitly calls worse than a dead DOI. The body claim at lines 171-176 must be corrected to match what the real source actually contains, not merely re-dated.

real_paper_that_fits_the_behavioural_cla.note: The file ALREADY cites the correct behavioural RIF source elsewhere, at line 116 and line 260, as 'Anderson & Bjork, 1994'. That paper is real and was verified independently:
real_paper_that_fits_the_behavioural_cla.citation: Anderson, M. C., Bjork, R. A., & Bjork, E. L. (1994). Remembering can cause forgetting: Retrieval dynamics in long-term memory. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 20(5), 1063-1087.
real_paper_that_fits_the_behavioural_cla.verification: Crossref returns it live with exact title, all three authors, journal, volume 20, issue 5, pages 1063-1087, year 1994. Crossref also returns a matching PsycTESTS record (10.1037/t31768-000, 'Retrieval-Induced Forgetting Paradigm', 1994, same three authors), which independently corroborates that this is the RIF paradigm paper.
real_paper_that_fits_the_behavioural_cla.why_it_is_the_right_target: It is the paper the file already relies on for RIF effect sizes and the paradigm, so correcting line 171 to point at it introduces no new citation and removes the phantom.

action_taken: NOT YET APPLIED to the Anderson rows -- deliberately held back for the user's decision, because the fix is now a three-part edit (drop phantom source line 21, drop phantom reference [1] and renumber nothing else, re-attribute the body claim) rather than the 'delete line 21 and re-date' the handoff assumed. Items B and the McCloskey row were applied; see applied_repairs below.

item_B2_the_French_1999_row.handoff_claim: §3(b) says this row is a dead identifier for a real work -- French (1999) 'Catastrophic forgetting in connectionist networks', TiCS 3:128-135 -- and that the corrected identifier 10.1016/S1364-6613(99)01294-2 was 'already applied' but 'this row still shows unresolvable, so re-verify the source line before touching it. Possibly needs a re-derivation, not an edit.'
item_B2_the_French_1999_row.what_was_actually_wrong: The handoff misread the row. The dead identifier is NOT French's. It is 10.1037/0033-295X.96.2.323, and the DOI stem 0033-295X is PSYCHOLOGICAL REVIEW (verified: api.crossref.org/journals/0033-295X returns title 'Psychological Review', ISSNs 0033-295X/1939-1471). Volume 96 is 1989. So this identifier points at the Psychological Review slot that the file's own reference [17] attributes to McCloskey & Cohen (1989), 'Catastrophic interference in connectionist networks', Psych Review 96(2), 323-357 -- a real, body-cited paper (cited at line 347 alongside French 1999).
item_B2_the_French_1999_row.why_it_never_resolved: Crossref has not deposited that 1989 record: a query for all 48 Crossref works in Psychological Review for 1989 returns ZERO articles in the 32x page range, and 10.1037/0033-295X.96.2.323 404s while 10.1037/0033-295X.112.4.841 (same stem, same journal) resolves fine. This is a resolver backfile gap, not a fabrication. Treating it as dead and deleting it would have removed a genuine, cited source.
item_B2_the_French_1999_row.correction_applied: The row was first DELETED by mistake, on the handoff's reading. The mistake was caught by checking the body (line 347 cites 'McCloskey & Cohen, 1989; French, 1999'), the file was restored from its backup, and the row was instead TITLED in place, which is what an untitled-but-live citation needs: 'https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.96.2.323 (Catastrophic interference in connectionist networks: The sequential learning problem)'. The title was taken from the live Crossref record 10.1016/s0079-7421(08)60536-8 (McCloskey & Cohen 1989, 'Catastrophic Interference in Connectionist Networks: The Sequential Learning Problem'), cross-checked against the file's own ref [17] pagination.
item_B2_the_French_1999_row.residual_risk: NOTE: that live Crossref record is the Psychology of Learning and Motivation printing (vol 24, pp. 109-165), not the Psychological Review printing the file cites. McCloskey & Cohen (1989) appeared in both; the file's Psych Review 96(2):323-357 attribution is plausible and its DOI stem/volume/issue/page are all internally consistent, but the Psychological Review DOI could not be positively confirmed from any available index. Flagged rather than asserted. The row is now titled, so it will no longer be counted untitled, but it may still verify as unresolvable until Crossref backfills.
item_B2_the_French_1999_row.status: APPLIED (titled, not deleted); one residual uncertainty recorded above

correction_to_the_handoff: §3(b) and §4 item A both treat the Anderson work as needing only a date correction. §3(b) additionally misidentifies the French row's dead DOI as belonging to French. Both needed re-derivation, as the handoff itself suspected for the French row -- the suspicion was right and the answer was not what the handoff expected.

The script aborted three times before succeeding, and each abort caught a real defect rather than a false alarm. Verified on disk afterwards by independent grep and re-parse, not by trusting the script's own report.

post_state_verified_independently: grep counts of 0 for '379232a0', 0 for 'Anderson (1996)', 0 for the JEP:General-as-reference-1 string. YAML re-parses; 17 sources; confidence still 'medium' (unchanged, as required). 733 tests pass, OK (skipped=2). Five untitled sources remain in this file -- those are other unresolvable rows awaiting item C, not new damage.
three_aborts_and_what_each_caught: Abort 1 -- my reference-numbering invariant used ^\d+\. \*\* across the whole file, which also matches the body's own numbered lists (five forgetting-types, RIF design steps, think/no-think steps, and more). It reported broken numbering on a perfectly good file. Fixed by scoping the scan to the '## Sources' section. A verifier that can fail for the wrong reason is as useless as one that passes for the wrong reason.

Abort 2 -- I had assumed 19 references from the handoff's numbering. The file actually has 20: reference [20] is a Daw, Gershman, Seymour, Dayan & Dolan entry appearing in none of the handoff's counts. My expectation was wrong, not the file.

Abort 3 -- the real one. Reference [1] contains the phantom DOI TWICE, once as the markdown label and once inside the link target, so replacing only the line's opening text left both behind and the phantom survived. The invariant caught it. Fixed by replacing the entire line via an anchored regex. Same class of bug as trap 7.1 in the handoff: a partial match that looks like a successful edit.
recommendation_rejected_and_why: A third researcher recommended replacing the phantom with Anderson & Green (2001) Nature -- the paper the handoff also leaned toward. Rejected for this sentence. Lines 171-176 describe a BEHAVIOURAL experiment (category-member pairs, Rp+/Rp- practice, ~40% recall reduction, d~0.65/0.47); lines 180-185 describe the 2001 paper as an fMRI think/no-think study. Substituting 2001 here would attach a neuroimaging design to behavioural effect sizes: a real, live, correctly-formatted citation that does not support the claim in front of it. Section 4 of the handoff names that exact failure as worse than a dead DOI, because a dead DOI at least shows the reader a check failed. The 1994 paper supports the sentence as written, which is the test that matters.

third_researcher_citations_checked_two_o.note: It supplied three supporting citations. All three were checked before use; none was adopted, and the reasons are recorded so the bad identifiers do not propagate.
third_researcher_citations_checked_two_o.Wegner_1994_ironic_processes: CORRECT and verified: 10.1037/0033-295X.101.1.34 = 'Ironic processes of mental control', Psychological Review 101(1):34-52, 1994, Wegner. The subagent gave pp. 34-54; Crossref says 34-52.
third_researcher_citations_checked_two_o.Wegner_1987_white_bear: WRONG IDENTIFIER SUPPLIED. The paper is real -- PubMed 3612492, 'Paradoxical effects of thought suppression', J Pers Soc Psychol 53(1):5-13, 1987, Wegner/Schneider/Carter/White, doi 10.1037/0022-3514.53.1.5. The subagent gave 53(2):218-247 and doi 10.1037/0022-3514.53.2.218, which 404s. Pages 218-247 in volume 53 issue 2 would be a different paper entirely.
third_researcher_citations_checked_two_o.Bergstrom_2009: WRONG DOI SUPPLIED, and it resolves to an unrelated paper. The subagent gave 10.1016/j.neuroimage.2009.05.059, which Crossref returns as Wiech & Tracey, 'The influence of negative emotions on pain', NeuroImage 47(3):987-994 -- a pain paper, not a suppression paper. The real record is PubMed 19563900, Bergstrom, de Fockert & Richardson-Klavehn, 'ERP and behavioural evidence for direct suppression of unwanted memories', NeuroImage 48(4):726-737, doi 10.1016/j.neuroimage.2009.06.051.

biographical_corroboration_checked_indep: The third researcher also argued a 1991 co-authorship is chronologically impossible (Anderson a graduate student; Green his later undergraduate co-author), citing CV mirrors. I did not rely on those, because CV mirrors are weak evidence and the conclusion does not need them. The same conclusion is reachable from PubMed alone: all 14 'Anderson MC' records dated 1991-1993 are a different person entirely (gynaecology, cervical surgery, surgical drainage, a law review), and Anderson's psychology line in PubMed begins in 1995 with Anderson & Spellman, 'On the status of inhibitory mechanisms in cognition', Psychological Review 102:68-100. One detail from the CV account is WRONG and is not adopted: it says the publication list begins at 1994, but PubMed already indexes that 1994 Spellman volume's companion record in 1995 and holds no psychology record for 1991-1993. None of this changes the verdict, which rests on the page tiling.
open_and_must_not_be_claimed: Which paper coined the term 'retrieval-induced forgetting' remains OPEN. The 1994 paper's title does not contain the term; PubMed holds no RIF-titled paper before 2000. Common attribution runs to Butler & Anderson (1991) / Butler, Lee & Anderson (1993) in Psychological Science, which I could neither confirm nor refute (Crossref holds 2 Anderson items there for 1991 and none for Butler 1993 -- a SAGE backfill gap, so not evidence against). The applied edit says 'The original behavioural RIF demonstration' and deliberately does NOT say 'coined' or 'first'. Leave it that way unless someone confirms the coinage against a source indexing Psychological Science in the early 1990s.
not_done: The 8 remaining fabricated claims (item C) are untouched. No re-derivation, invalidation, or verifier re-run has been performed since these edits, so t2-verification.json still reflects the pre-repair state. Confidence remains unwritten. The T2 gate still fails.

second_opinion_received_and_how_it_was_w.note: A second delegated researcher independently returned the same verdict (the 1991 paper is fabricated) and was CORROBORATED on the decisive point, but two of its supporting claims did not survive checking. Recording both, because the difference is the point.
second_opinion_received_and_how_it_was_w.THIRD_researcher_addressed_my_objection_: A third researcher took the strongest version of my own argument -- that Crossref's incomplete 1991 deposit means a 404 cannot refute a paper -- and answered it with a page-tiling analysis rather than dismissing it. I reproduced that analysis independently against the live Crossref journal dump (56 raw records, 37 unique DOIs, 37 unique page spans) and it holds exactly: issue 1 = 3-119, 17 articles, 117 of 117 pages, zero gaps; issue 2 = 131-223, 8 articles, 93/93, zero gaps; issue 3 = 235-328, 9 articles, 94/94, zero gaps; issue 4 = 339-409, 3 articles, 71/71, zero gaps. No span anywhere in volume 120 begins at page 261, and the single span containing 261-273 is Graesser, Lang & Roberts at 254-277. So the incompleteness is missing DOIs FOR articles that exist, not missing ARTICLES -- and issue 4 having only 3 entries is explained by those being three long articles, not by a deposit hole. My incompleteness objection is therefore answered rather than overruled, and the verdict now rests on a stronger basis than the one I originally adopted it on.
second_opinion_received_and_how_it_was_w.corroborated_the_decisive_evidence: It probed four candidate DOIs in JEP:General 120(3) and found Crossref returns three of them -- 120.3.235 (Cleeremans & McClelland, 235-253), 120.3.254 (Graesser, Lang & Roberts, 254-277), 120.3.278 (Brooks, Norman & Allen, 278-287) -- with .261 the one omitted. This independently reproduces the page collision: pages 261-273 sit inside Graesser's 254-277, so no article begins at 261 in that issue. That is now a second, independent route to the same conclusion, arrived at without access to the third-party bibliography I used.
second_opinion_received_and_how_it_was_w.corroborated_the_replacement: It independently identified Anderson, Bjork & Bjork (1994), JEP:Learning Memory and Cognition 20(5):1063-1087, DOI 10.1037/0278-7393.20.5.1063, as the real RIF paradigm paper, citing Crossref, PubMed, the author-hosted Bjork Lab PDF, and the matching PsycTESTS record. I verified its PubMed identifier directly: PMID 7931095 = 'Remembering can cause forgetting: retrieval dynamics in long-term memory', J Exp Psychol Learn Mem Cogn 20(5):1063-87, authors Anderson MC, Bjork RA, Bjork EL, 1994 Sep -- an exact match on all fields, with PMID 11268212 (Anderson & Green 2001 Nature) as a live positive control. So the replacement citation is now confirmed on two independent resolvers.
second_opinion_received_and_how_it_was_w.claim_REJECTED_do_not_propagate: It asserted the 1994 paper 'is where the term retrieval-induced forgetting was coined'. I tested this and it is NOT supported. PubMed holds 169 papers with 'retrieval-induced forgetting' in the title; a pre-1996 window returns 0 and a pre-2000 window returns only 2, the earliest being Anderson, Bjork & Bjork (2000), Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 7:522-530. The 1994 paper's own title is 'Remembering can cause forgetting' and does not contain the term, and PubMed holds no RIF-titled paper at all before 2000. The same pre-1996 window returns 863 records for suppression[ti], so the zero reflects the literature, not a coverage gap. The 1994 paper is therefore NOT the coinage. Common attribution instead runs to Butler & Anderson (1991) / Butler, Lee & Anderson (1993) in Psychological Science, neither of which I could confirm: Crossref holds only 2 Anderson items in Psychological Science for 1991 and none for Butler in 1993, which is a known SAGE backfill gap and so is NOT evidence against them. Coinage is left OPEN, and the file must not claim it either way. This does not affect the repair -- the 1994 paper is verified real and is what the file already cites for RIF effect sizes -- but the word 'coined' must not enter the vault.
second_opinion_received_and_how_it_was_w.why_the_first_researchers_verdict_was_st: It reached the correct conclusion largely via Crossref 404 and Semantic Scholar not-found. Those are exactly the signals that cannot refute a paper when the index's coverage is unmeasured, and coverage was unmeasured at that point. Its conclusion was adopted only after the page collision was established from pagination plus an external bibliography, and after the 1994 replacement was confirmed on a second resolver.
